summary: Factors, multiples and divisibility rules, reasoned without heavy arithmetic.
ideas: n is divisible by d when n = d·k for some integer k. Every non-zero integer divides 0.

Divisibility rules: 2 (last digit even), 3 (digit sum divisible by 3), 4 (last two digits divisible by 4), 5 (ends in 0 or 5), 6 (by 2 and by 3), 8 (last three digits divisible by 8), 9 (digit sum divisible by 9), 11 (alternating digit sum divisible by 11).
If d divides a and d divides b, then d divides a + b and a − b.
The product of k consecutive integers is divisible by k! (for example, three consecutive integers: by 6).
For positive integers a and b: GCD(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b.
formulas: Multiples of k from 1 to n: ⌊n/k⌋
Multiples of k from a to b (inclusive): ⌊b/k⌋ − ⌊(a − 1)/k⌋
method: Translate “divisible by”, “multiple of”, “factor of” into n = d·k.
Break every number into prime factors before reasoning.
Check what the question allows: integer? positive? distinct?
Test a few real numbers to confirm a pattern before trusting it.
traps: 0 is a multiple of every integer, and multiples can be negative.
“Integer” does not mean “positive integer”.
If a + b is divisible by d, a and b are not necessarily divisible by d (3 + 7 is divisible by 5).
shortcuts: To test divisibility by a composite number, test coprime factors: divisible by 12 ⇔ divisible by 3 and by 4.

example.q: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 6 but not by 4?
example.a: Multiples of 6: ⌊100/6⌋ = 16. Those also divisible by 4 are the multiples of LCM(6, 4) = 12: ⌊100/12⌋ = 8. Answer: 16 − 8 = **8** (6, 18, 30, 42, 54, 66, 78, 90).

summary: Prime factorisation and everything it unlocks: divisors, GCD, LCM, factorials.
ideas: A prime has exactly two positive divisors. 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
Every integer greater than 1 has one prime factorisation.
If n = p^{a}·q^{b}·r^{c}, n has (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1) positive divisors.
Perfect squares have only even exponents and an odd number of divisors.
GCD: common primes with the lowest exponents. LCM: all primes with the highest exponents.
formulas: Exponent of prime p in n!: ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p^{2}⌋ + ⌊n/p^{3}⌋ + …
method: Factorise every number into primes first.
Compare exponents prime by prime.
Read carefully: “distinct prime factors” counts each prime once.
traps: Forgetting that 2 is prime, or treating 1 as prime.
Counting prime factors when the question asks for all divisors.
Mixing “distinct prime factors” with prime factors counted with repetition.
shortcuts: To check whether a number up to 100 is prime, test only the primes 2, 3, 5, 7.

example.q: How many positive divisors does 360 have?

summary: n = d·q + r: remainders, their arithmetic and the cycles of units digits.
ideas: Dividing n by d: n = d·q + r with 0 ≤ r < d. If the remainder is r, then n − r is a multiple of d.
Remainders add and multiply: the remainder of a + b (or a·b) is the remainder of the remainders’ sum (or product).
Units digits of powers repeat: 2 → 2, 4, 8, 6; 3 → 3, 9, 7, 1; 7 → 7, 9, 3, 1; 4 → 4, 6; 9 → 9, 1; 0, 1, 5, 6 stay the same.
If n is smaller than d, the remainder is n itself (3 ÷ 7 leaves 3).
method: Write n = d·q + r and list the first values: r, r + d, r + 2d, …
With two conditions, find the smallest number that meets both; the rest repeat every LCM of the divisors.
For big powers, find the cycle length and divide the exponent by it.
traps: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and can be 0.
Remainder questions often hide the fact that n can be small (n = r is allowed).
shortcuts: Units digit of 7^{n}: cycle of 4, so use the remainder of n ÷ 4 (remainder 0 means the 4th term).

example.q: n leaves remainder 3 when divided by 5 and remainder 2 when divided by 7. What is the remainder when n is divided by 35?
example.a: Numbers with remainder 3 mod 5: 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, … The first with remainder 2 mod 7 is 23 (23 = 21 + 2). So n = 23 + 35k and the remainder is **23**.

summary: Parity and sign rules that settle “must be true” questions fast.
ideas: even ± even = even; odd ± odd = even; even ± odd = odd.
A product is even if at least one factor is even; odd × odd = odd.
A product or quotient is negative exactly when it has an odd number of negative factors.
Even powers are never negative; odd powers keep the sign of the base.
0 is even, and neither positive nor negative.
method: Rewrite the expression by factoring (ab + a = a(b + 1)).
Test cases: one even and one odd, one positive and one negative, and 0.
For “must be true”, one counterexample is enough to eliminate a choice.
traps: Fractions are neither even nor odd; parity rules apply to integers only.
x^{2} > x is false for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.
Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it.
shortcuts: “Odd × anything even = even” settles most product questions in one line.

example.q: a and b are integers and ab + a is odd. Which must be true?
example.a: ab + a = a(b + 1). A product is odd only if both factors are odd, so a is odd and b + 1 is odd: **a is odd and b is even**.

summary: Comparing, simplifying and converting fractions without a calculator.
ideas: Compare two positive fractions by cross-multiplying: a/b > c/d ⇔ ad > bc.
Adding the same positive number to numerator and denominator moves a positive fraction toward 1.
A fraction in lowest terms has a terminating decimal exactly when its denominator has no primes other than 2 and 5.
Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive number larger.
method: Keep fractions as fractions through multi-step work; convert at the end.
Cancel common factors before multiplying.
Reduce a fraction fully before judging whether its decimal terminates.
traps: 21/60 looks non-terminating because of the 3, but it reduces to 7/20, which terminates.
Rounding early makes answer choices look equal.
shortcuts: Benchmark with 1/2 or 1 to compare fractions without computing them.

example.q: Which of 7/15, 21/60 and 13/42 has a terminating decimal?
example.a: 7/15: denominator 3·5, no. 21/60 = 7/20: denominator 2^{2}·5, **yes**. 13/42: denominator 2·3·7, no.

summary: Exponent rules, factoring powers and handling roots.
ideas: a^{0} = 1 (a ≠ 0); a^{−n} = 1/a^{n}; a^{1/n} is the n-th root.
You cannot combine a sum of powers directly; factor the smallest power: 2^{10} + 2^{11} = 2^{10}(1 + 2) = 3·2^{10}.
√(x^{2}) = |x|. The √ symbol always gives the non-negative root.
For 0 < x < 1, higher powers are smaller: x^{3} < x^{2} < x < √x.
method: Rewrite everything with the same base (4 = 2^{2}, 8 = 2^{3}, 27 = 3^{3}).
Factor out the smallest power in sums and differences.
To compare powers, match either the bases or the exponents.
traps: A negative base with an even exponent gives a positive result: (−2)^{4} = 16, but −2^{4} = −16.
x^{2} = 9 has two solutions, ±3; √9 is only 3.
shortcuts: Simplify roots by pulling out squares: √72 = √(36·2) = 6√2.

summary: Percent change, successive changes and reverse percents with multipliers.
ideas: An increase of p% multiplies by (1 + p/100); a decrease of p% multiplies by (1 − p/100).
Successive changes multiply: +25% then −20% is 1.25 × 0.80 = 1.00, no net change.
Percent change = (new − old) / old × 100. The base is always the original value.
Percentage points measure differences between percents: from 10% to 12% is +2 points but +20%.
“x is what percent of y” is x/y × 100.
method: Pick 100 as the starting value when no number is given.
Turn every change into a multiplier and multiply them.
For reverse percents, divide by the multiplier: after a 20% rise to 60, the original is 60/1.2 = 50.
traps: Adding successive percents (+20% then −20% is not 0%).
Using the new value as the base of a percent change.
Confusing percent with percentage points.
shortcuts: 10% is moving the decimal point; 5% is half of that; 15% = 10% + 5%.

example.q: A price rises 25% and then falls 20%. What is the overall percent change?
example.a: 1.25 × 0.80 = 1.00: the final price equals the original, so the change is **0%**.

summary: Ratios as parts of a whole, combining ratios and proportions.
ideas: a : b = m : n means a = m·k and b = n·k for some positive k.
Part-to-whole: a is m/(m + n) of the total.
To combine a : b and b : c, rescale so b matches: 2 : 3 and 4 : 5 give 8 : 12 : 15.
Direct proportion: y = kx. Inverse proportion: xy = k.
formulas: a : b = m : n ⇒ a = mk, b = nk
method: Write each quantity as a multiple of an unknown k.
Use the total or a change to find k.
Answer the quantity actually asked for.
traps: A ratio is not the actual numbers: 3 : 5 could be 30 and 50.
Part-to-part and part-to-whole give different fractions.
When amounts are added, the ratio changes; set up a new equation.
shortcuts: If the total must be a whole number, it must be a multiple of the sum of the ratio parts.

example.q: The ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 5. After 6 boys join, the ratio is 1 : 1. How many girls are there?
example.a: Boys = 3k, girls = 5k. 3k + 6 = 5k gives k = 3, so there are **15 girls**.

summary: Distance, speed and time; combined work rates.
ideas: Distance = rate × time; work = rate × time.
Average speed = total distance / total time, not the average of the speeds.
Objects moving toward each other: add speeds. Same direction: subtract them.
Work rates add: a job done in a hours has rate 1/a per hour.
Two workers together: time = ab/(a + b).
formulas: Equal distances at v₁ and v₂: average speed = 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂)
method: Write the rate of each person or machine per unit of time.
Add rates for people working together (subtract for a drain working against a fill).
Keep units consistent: minutes or hours, not both.
traps: Averaging two speeds for equal distances.
Mixing minutes and hours.
Adding times instead of rates.
shortcuts: A rate table (rate · time = distance/work) keeps multi-part problems organised.

example.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours, pipe B in 3 hours. How long do they take together?
example.a: Rates: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 tank per hour, so **2 hours** (or 6·3/(6 + 3) = 2).

summary: Tracking the pure ingredient and weighted averages of concentrations.
ideas: Amount of pure substance = concentration × total volume.
Adding water changes the total but not the amount of solute.
The concentration of a mix is the weighted average of the concentrations.
Alligation: the quantities mixed are in inverse ratio to their distances from the final concentration.
method: Track the pure ingredient before and after.
Write the new concentration as (new amount of ingredient) / (new total).
For two solutions mixed, use a weighted average or alligation.
traps: Forgetting that the total volume changes.
Averaging percentages without weighting by volume.
shortcuts: If the target is exactly halfway between two concentrations, mix equal amounts.

example.q: How many litres of water must be added to 10 L of a 30% salt solution to get a 20% solution?
example.a: Salt: 0.3 × 10 = 3 L, which does not change. 3 / (10 + x) = 0.2 gives 10 + x = 15, so **5 L**.

summary: Simple and compound interest.
ideas: Simple interest: I = P·r·t (interest only on the principal).
Compound interest: A = P(1 + r/n)^{nt}, where n is the number of compounding periods per year.
Over more than one period, compound interest earns more than simple interest at the same rate.
Two years at r compounded yearly: P(1 + r)^{2} = P(1 + 2r + r^{2}); the extra r^{2} is interest on interest.
method: Identify the rate per period and the number of periods.
Semiannual means r/2, twice a year; quarterly means r/4, four times a year.
Estimate first: compound interest is slightly more than simple interest.
traps: Using the annual rate for each semiannual period.
Forgetting to subtract the principal when asked for interest earned.
shortcuts: For small rates over a few periods, compound ≈ simple + a small extra; use that to eliminate choices.

example.q: $1,000 is invested at 10% a year, compounded semiannually. What is it worth after 1 year?

summary: Two- and three-set problems with formulas and the double-set matrix.
ideas: Two sets: Total = A + B − Both + Neither.
Three sets: Total = A + B + C − (A∩B + A∩C + B∩C) + A∩B∩C + Neither.
With “exactly two” counts: Total = A + B + C − (exactly two) − 2·(all three) + Neither.
Two yes/no attributes (e.g. gender and smoker) fit a 2 × 2 table with totals.
method: Decide whether the problem uses “both/at least two” or “exactly two”.
For two attributes, draw the 2 × 2 table and fill the cells you know.
Solve for the missing cell or overlap.
traps: Counting the overlap twice.
Mixing “exactly two” with “at least two”.
Forgetting the “neither” group.
shortcuts: In a 2 × 2 table every row and column must add up; fill the easiest cell first.

example.q: Of 50 students, 30 study French, 25 study Spanish and 10 study neither. How many study both?

summary: Mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation.
ideas: Mean = sum / number of values, so sum = mean × number.
Median: the middle value of the ordered list; with an even count, the average of the two middle values.
Range = maximum − minimum.
Standard deviation measures spread around the mean: adding a constant to every value does not change it; multiplying every value by k multiplies it by |k|; it is 0 only when all values are equal.
In an evenly spaced set, mean = median = (first + last)/2.
method: Convert means to sums as soon as values are added or removed.
Sort the list before finding a median.
For standard deviation, compare how far values sit from the mean; you rarely need to compute it.
traps: Taking the median of an unsorted list.
Assuming mean and median are equal in a set that is not evenly spaced.
Thinking a larger mean means a larger standard deviation.
shortcuts: Adding a value equal to the mean keeps the mean and does not increase the standard deviation.

example.q: The mean of 5 numbers is 12. If the number 20 is removed, what is the mean of the rest?
example.a: Sum = 60. Without 20: 40, over 4 numbers: **10**.

summary: Multiplication principle, permutations, combinations and restrictions.
ideas: Multiplication principle: independent choices multiply.
Order matters → permutations: n!/(n − k)!. Order does not matter → combinations: C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!).
Arrangements with identical items: n!/(a!·b!·…).
Around a circle: (n − 1)! arrangements.
Complement: count everything, then subtract what is not allowed.
method: Ask: does order matter? Are there repetitions? Any restrictions?
Handle restrictions first (fixed seats, items that must be together).
For “items together”, treat them as one block, then multiply by their internal arrangements.
traps: Using permutations for teams or committees (order does not matter).
Double counting when choosing in stages.
Forgetting the internal order of a block.
shortcuts: C(n, k) = C(n, n − k): choosing who is in equals choosing who is out.

example.q: In how many ways can 5 people sit in a row if A and B must sit next to each other?
example.a: Treat AB as one block: 4 units → 4! = 24 orders, and A, B can swap inside the block: 24 × 2 = **48**.

summary: Equally likely outcomes, complements, independent events and “at least one”.
ideas: P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes (when outcomes are equally likely).
P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B).
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Without replacement, the probabilities change after each draw.
formulas: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
method: Decide whether draws are with or without replacement.
For “at least one”, compute 1 − P(none).
For a specific sequence, multiply step by step; if order does not matter, multiply by the number of orders.
traps: Adding probabilities of events that can happen together.
Forgetting to multiply by the number of possible orders.
Treating dependent draws as independent.
shortcuts: A probability is never above 1: use that to eliminate answer choices.

example.q: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of at least one head?
example.a: P(no heads) = (1/2)^{3} = 1/8, so P(at least one head) = **7/8**.

summary: Arithmetic and geometric sequences, sums and recursive rules.
ideas: Arithmetic: a_{n} = a_{1} + (n − 1)d; sum = n(a_{1} + a_{n})/2.
Geometric: a_{n} = a_{1}·r^{n−1}.
Number of terms from a to b in steps of d: (b − a)/d + 1.
Recursive rules (a_{n} defined from a_{n−1}): compute the first terms and look for a pattern or cycle.
method: Identify the type: constant difference or constant ratio?
Count terms carefully (inclusive counts add 1).
For sums of evenly spaced numbers, use average × count.
traps: Off-by-one errors: n − 1 in the formula, +1 when counting inclusively.
Assuming a pattern after only two terms.
shortcuts: Sum of evenly spaced numbers = average of first and last × number of terms.

example.q: What is the sum of the integers from 20 to 80, inclusive?

summary: Systems of linear equations and translating words into equations.
ideas: You usually need as many independent equations as unknowns.
Solve by substitution or elimination.
A system can have one solution, none (parallel lines) or infinitely many (the same line).
Sometimes the question asks for a combination (like x + y) that you can get without finding each variable.
method: Write down exactly what is asked.
Look for a combination of the equations that gives it directly.
Otherwise eliminate one variable and solve.
traps: Assuming two equations always give a unique solution (2x + 2y = 4 and x + y = 2 are the same line).
Reversing “less than”: 5 less than x is x − 5.
shortcuts: Adding or subtracting the equations often isolates the combination the question asks for.

example.q: 3x + 2y = 12 and x − y = −1. What is x?
example.a: From the second equation x = y − 1. Substitute: 3(y − 1) + 2y = 12, so y = 3 and **x = 2**.

summary: Factoring quadratics, special products, roots and function notation.
ideas: x^{2} + bx + c = (x − r₁)(x − r₂) with r₁ + r₂ = −b and r₁·r₂ = c.
For ax^{2} + bx + c: sum of roots = −b/a, product = c/a.
The discriminant b^{2} − 4ac tells how many real roots there are: > 0 two, = 0 one, < 0 none.
Function notation: f(3) means replace x by 3; f(g(x)) means apply g first.
method: Move everything to one side and factor.
Recognise special products instantly.
Never divide both sides by a variable that could be 0.
traps: Dividing x^{2} = 5x by x loses the root x = 0.
Forgetting the negative root of x^{2} = k.
shortcuts: a^{2} − b^{2} = (a + b)(a − b) turns big arithmetic into easy products: 51^{2} − 49^{2} = 100 × 2 = 200.

example.q: If x^{2} − 5x + 6 = 0, what is the sum of all possible values of x^{2}?
example.a: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 2 or 3. Sum of squares: 4 + 9 = **13**.

summary: Solving inequalities, sign flips and absolute value as distance.
ideas: Multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the inequality.
Do not multiply by a variable unless you know its sign.
|x| is the distance from 0: |x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b; |x − a| > b ⇔ x < a − b or x > a + b.
Inequalities pointing the same way can be added, never subtracted.
formulas: |x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b
method: Isolate the variable, flipping the sign when you divide by a negative.
For absolute values, read them as distances on a number line.
Test the boundary points and one value on each side.
traps: Squaring both sides when negatives are possible.
|x| = −x when x < 0, a frequent Data Sufficiency trap.
Strict (<) versus inclusive (≤) boundaries when counting integers.
shortcuts: Draw the number line: the answer is usually visible at once.

example.a: −4 < x − 3 < 4, so −1 < x < 7: the integers 0 to 6, that is **7**.

summary: Translating English into equations and checking the answer.
ideas: “is” means =, “of” means ×, “more than” means +, “less than” reverses the order (5 less than x is x − 5).
Age problems: the difference between two ages never changes.
Profit = revenue − cost; markup is on cost, discount is on the selling price.
Answer choices are a tool: backsolving is often faster than algebra.
method: Read the question last sentence first: what exactly is asked?
Name the variables and write the equations.
Solve, then check the result against the story.
If the algebra is messy, backsolve starting from the middle answer choice.
traps: Solving for the wrong quantity (the other person’s age, the original price).
Reversing “less than”.
Mixing units.
shortcuts: Backsolving: try the middle choice; if it is too small, move to larger choices.

example.q: Tom is 4 years older than twice Ann’s age. In 6 years the sum of their ages will be 58. How old is Ann now?
